options: It walks through a table row by row, evaluating an expression for each row before combining the results
It only works on numeric columns
It can only be used inside CALCULATE
It automatically creates a calculated column
questions.explain: Iterator functions (SUMX, AVERAGEX, COUNTX, and others) evaluate an expression per row across a table, rather than aggregating a single column directly.

questions.q: In 'Total Revenue = SUMX(Sales, Sales[Quantity] * Sales[UnitPrice])', why can't a plain SUM be used instead?
options: Because the value being summed doesn't exist as a single column — it must be calculated per row first
Because SUM can't be used in measures
Because SUMX is always faster than SUM
Because Sales[Quantity] and Sales[UnitPrice] are in different tables
questions.explain: SUM aggregates one existing column directly. SUMX evaluates Quantity times UnitPrice fresh for every row, then sums those per-row results — something SUM alone can't express.

questions.q: What visual cue identifies an iterator function by name?
options: It ends in the letter X, like SUMX, AVERAGEX, or COUNTX
It starts with the word ITERATE
It's always written in lowercase
It always takes exactly one argument
questions.explain: Every iterator function follows the same naming pattern: the base aggregation name plus an X suffix.

questions.q: What does combining SUMX with FILTER let you do that SUM alone can't?
options: Sum a column, but only across rows matching a complex condition
Sum two different tables at once
Create a new relationship between tables
Convert a measure into a calculated column
questions.explain: FILTER can build a table expression restricted to rows meeting a condition, which SUMX then iterates over — expressing 'sum this, but only for rows where...'

questions.q: When should you reach for an iterator instead of a plain aggregation function?
options: When the value needs to be calculated fresh per row, rather than already existing as one column
Always — iterators should replace plain aggregations in every formula
Only when working with text columns
Only inside calculated columns, never inside measures
questions.explain: If the number already exists as a single column, plain SUM/AVERAGE/COUNT is simpler. Iterators earn their place when a value must be computed row by row first.
